books.section: Great Depression and the New Deal (1929-1939)

source: original; documents drawn from public-domain sources, paraphrases, and book-grounded data
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the New Deal affected different groups of Americans in different ways from 1933 to 1939.

documents.title: The CCC and young men
documents.source: Paraphrase of 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 23, and Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, Topic 7.10.
documents.text: Paraphrase: The Civilian Conservation Corps gave young men between 18 and 24 work on forest and conservation projects, and eventually employed more than 2.5 million of them. Most of their small pay was mailed home to their families. The Corps took young men only; it excluded women.
documents.sourcing: A textbook account of the CCC, written long after the events. A summary of who the program served, not a worker's own words.

documents.title: The AAA and sharecroppers
documents.source: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, Topic 7.10.
documents.text: Paraphrase: The Agricultural Adjustment Act paid farmers to grow fewer crops so that prices would rise. To cut output, landowners often evicted sharecroppers and took that land out of cultivation. That hurt many of the nation's poorest farmers, including numerous African-American farmers.
documents.sourcing: A textbook account of the AAA's side effects, written long after the events. A summary of who lost land, not a sharecropper's own words.

documents.title: The Indian Reorganization Act
documents.source: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, Topic 7.10.
documents.text: Paraphrase: The Indian Reorganization Act of 1934 largely undid the Dawes Act of 1887, which had broken up reservations into small plots for individual Indians. The new act restored tribal ownership of reservation lands, recognized tribal governments, and extended loans to Indian groups for economic development.
documents.sourcing: A textbook account of the act, written long after the events. A summary of the policy change, not a tribal voice.

documents.title: The Wagner Act and unions
documents.source: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, Topic 7.10.
documents.text: Paraphrase: The Wagner Act guaranteed workers the right to organize unions and bargain collectively, and it created the National Labor Relations Board to enforce the law. Union membership rose from about 3 million in 1933 to 10.5 million by 1941.
documents.sourcing: A textbook account of the Wagner Act, written long after the events. A summary of the law and its results, not a worker's own words.

documents.title: African Americans and the New Deal
documents.source: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, Topic 7.10.
documents.text: Paraphrase: African Americans were already vulnerable before the Depression, and many New Deal programs ignored them. Roosevelt, wary of losing the Southern wing of his party, did not push for civil rights or anti-lynching legislation. Yet Black voters shifted toward the Democrats, encouraged by Eleanor Roosevelt and Interior Secretary Harold Ickes, and by the Black Cabinet of Black advisers to the president. In 1939 Eleanor Roosevelt helped arrange Marian Anderson's concert at the Lincoln Memorial after the Daughters of the American Revolution barred Anderson from its hall.
documents.sourcing: A textbook account of the shift, written long after the events. A summary of both the limits and the gains, not a voice from the 1930s.

documents.title: Women and the New Deal
documents.source: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, Topic 7.10.
documents.text: Paraphrase: Women carried a double burden in the Depression, keeping food on the table while being scorned for taking a job away from a man. New Deal programs tended to slight women: the CCC excluded them, and the NIRA set lower wage levels for women than for men. Yet Frances Perkins became the first woman in the cabinet as secretary of labor, and more women were working outside the home in 1940 than in 1930.
documents.sourcing: A textbook account of women's experience, written long after the events. A summary that compares treatment and gains, not a woman's own words.

documents.title: Work Pays America
documents.source: Vera Bock, Work Pays America poster, Works Progress Administration, Federal Art Project, between 1936 and 1941. Public domain (U.S. federal government poster); Library of Congress cph.3b48737.
documents.text: The poster shows a farmer holding a rake and a worker holding a hammer shaking hands over a stalk of wheat, with the word PROSPERITY arched above the wheat and WORKS PROGRESS ADMINISTRATION printed across the bottom. The poster wording is the poster's own.
documents.sourcing: A government poster meant to build support for the WPA by showing farm and factory workers together. An image that sells a program, not a neutral record.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the New Deal affected different groups of Americans in different ways from 1933 to 1939, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the limited government of the 1920s, the Progressive era's earlier reforms, or the Panics of 1893 and 1907.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument, or background from a later century, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant evidence from at least three documents to support an argument.
rubric.notEarned: Naming documents without describing their content does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or describing them without tying them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the court-packing plan, the Wagner Act, the election of 1936, or the Indian Reorganization Act.
rubric.notEarned: A vague reference to the New Deal with no specific example does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document's author, purpose, audience, or historical situation, such as a textbook account written long after the events, or a government poster meant to build support for a program.
rubric.notEarned: Naming an author without explaining why the authorship matters does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the change by showing its limits, or weighing how far the change lasted.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: The New Deal affected different groups very differently: it opened doors for union workers and tribal governments while leaving sharecroppers, women, and many Black workers outside its protections.
Context: The Depression struck a country already divided by race, sex, and place, with farmers in debt, wealth piled at the top, and Black and Mexican-American workers already at the edge of the economy.
Evidence: Documents 1-2 show the split in the First New Deal: the CCC gave more than 2.5 million young men work but excluded women, while the AAA paid landowners to cut output and evicted sharecroppers, many of them Black.
Evidence: Documents 3-4 show gains for two groups: the Indian Reorganization Act restored tribal land and governments, and the Wagner Act helped union membership rise from 3 million to 10.5 million.
Evidence: Documents 5-7 show a mixed record: Black voters shifted toward the Democrats despite no civil rights laws, women gained a cabinet secretary but faced lower NIRA wages, and the WPA poster promised work to farm and factory workers alike.
Beyond the documents: the Social Security Act first left out farm and domestic workers, and the TVA brought electricity to a poor region, showing the same uneven pattern.
Sourcing: the textbook accounts summarize long after the events, while the WPA poster was made to sell a program, so each document's purpose shapes what it shows.
Complexity: The differences were real but not absolute: hardship crossed group lines, since white-collar professionals lost jobs too, and some programs, like the WPA, hired across lines of work and place.
